en.title: Historical Formation of Caste Relations
en.summary: Caste relations in Mithila, Vajji and Anga were neither an unchanged survival from an ancient textual order nor a purely modern political invention. They were historical institutions repeatedly remade through marriage rules, genealogy, settlement, landholding, tenancy, labour, religious service, literacy, state employment, colonial enumeration, law, education and electoral representation.

mai.title: जाति-सम्बन्धक ऐतिहासिक निर्माण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “जाति-सम्बन्धक ऐतिहासिक निर्माण” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Caste relations must be reconstructed historically, not assumed as a timeless social essence
Varna and jati are related vocabularies but not interchangeable social maps
Early and medieval evidence is uneven, so later caste maps cannot be projected backward without proof
Settlement, specialised work and control over resources created local hierarchies long before modern administration

en.title: Dalit Histories
en.summary: Dalit history in Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be written as a footnote to the history of caste. It is a history of labour performed and appropriated, land possessed or denied, neighbourhoods segregated or opened, schools entered late and then used strategically, migration that loosened some village dependencies while creating new urban vulnerabilities, and public cultures through which communities named dignity in their own idioms.

mai.title: दलित इतिहास
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “दलित इतिहास” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Dalit history requires a vocabulary that separates legal category, historical stigma and political identity
The communities grouped as Scheduled Castes were never a single social or economic bloc
Landlessness converted social exclusion into material dependence
Musahar histories expose the long connection between stigma, landlessness and labour servitude

en.title: Adivasi and Forest-Connected Populations Where Regionally Relevant
en.summary: Adivasi history enters a history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga unevenly. The plains core of Mithila and Vajji cannot be represented as a continuous forest-tribal zone, while the eastern and south-eastern borderlands of Anga have long been connected to Santal, Paharia and other Adivasi histories through settlement, labour, forest margins, colonial administration and the former Bhagalpur-Santal Parganas geography.

mai.title: जहाँ क्षेत्रीय रूपसँ प्रासंगिक, आदिवासी आ वन-संलग्न जनसमूह
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “जहाँ क्षेत्रीय रूपसँ प्रासंगिक, आदिवासी आ वन-संलग्न जनसमूह” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Regional relevance must be demonstrated rather than assumed
Scheduled Tribe is a constitutional category with a specific legal history
Bihar’s Scheduled-Tribe population is significant at state scale but highly concentrated geographically
The Anga-eastern Bihar borderland is the principal Adivasi zone within this volume’s core geography

en.title: Muslims of Mithila and Anga
en.summary: The Muslim history of Mithila and Anga cannot be reduced to rulers, demographic percentages or moments of communal conflict. Muslim households entered the region’s social fabric through many routes: military and administrative service, scholarly and Sufi networks, agrarian settlement, artisanal production, trade, transport, migration and ordinary neighbourhood life.

mai.title: मिथिला आ अंगक मुसलमान
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मिथिला आ अंगक मुसलमान” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Muslim presence developed through several routes, not one “arrival” event
Sultanate and Bengal-facing frontiers produced layered rather than uniform political authority
Mughal-era revenue and road networks strengthened qasbas and service groups
Persian created an administrative and intellectual bridge across religious communities

en.title: Gender and the Household Economy
en.summary: A household is an economic institution before it is a statistical unit. It combines income, food, land, housing, care, credit, consumption, schooling, health expenditure, social obligations and protection against risk. Gender enters each of these domains through unequal claims on time, mobility, property, cash and authority. The relevant history is therefore not a story in which a self-contained ‘family’ slowly gives way to markets.

mai.title: लैंगिकता आ घरेलू अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “लैंगिकता आ घरेलू अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The household must be treated as an economic institution rather than a private residual
Household membership is not the same as equal membership in household resources
Agrarian households historically joined productive and reproductive work in the same social unit
Food management converted uncertain income into everyday security

en.title: Women’s Paid and Unpaid Labour
en.summary: Women’s labour is one of the clearest cases in which economic reality exceeds the boundaries of ordinary employment statistics. A woman may transplant paddy, tend cattle, sort makhana, assist a family loom, cook for a work gang, collect water and fuel, care for children and an elderly parent, keep household accounts and participate in a self-help group—all within the same week. Some of those activities generate wages or sales. Some produce goods for household use.

mai.title: महिलाक भुगतानित आ अपभुगतानित श्रम
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “महिलाक भुगतानित आ अपभुगतानित श्रम” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: “Work” and “employment” are not the same historical category
Colonial and early postcolonial enumeration repeatedly struggled with women’s subsidiary work
Agrarian labour made women indispensable while keeping tasks sharply gendered
Caste and class shaped whether women’s work was performed for wages, family production or status

en.title: Marriage, Dowry, Inheritance and Changing Family Structures
en.summary: Marriage is one of the institutions through which social hierarchy becomes household economy. It determines where people live, how labour is pooled, which kin are obligated to whom, how property moves across generations, and how status is displayed or contested. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, marriage has been reshaped by genealogy, caste and religious rules, landholding, education, migration, salaried employment, law, consumer markets and digital communication.

mai.title: विवाह, दहेज, उत्तराधिकार आ बदलैत पारिवारिक संरचना
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “विवाह, दहेज, उत्तराधिकार आ बदलैत पारिवारिक संरचना” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Marriage is an economic and political institution as well as a kinship relation
Historical family forms cannot be reconstructed by projecting the present backward
Genealogy made marriage regulation unusually visible in parts of Mithila
Marriage markets linked caste status to education, occupation and geography

en.title: Education and Social Mobility
en.summary: Education changes social history when learning and credentials alter who can enter occupations, migrate, speak to the state, postpone marriage, claim professional authority or imagine a life outside inherited work. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, this process has been neither linear nor equal.

mai.title: शिक्षा आ सामाजिक गतिशीलता
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “शिक्षा आ सामाजिक गतिशीलता” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Education is a mobility institution, not an automatic equaliser
Older learning systems were socially significant but narrow in reach
Colonial schooling made examinations convertible into new employment
Regional colleges reduced the geographical cost of higher learning

en.title: Reservation, Affirmative Action and New Middle Classes
en.summary: Reservation became one of the principal institutions through which the democratic state attempted to alter inherited inequalities in education, public employment and representation. In Bihar this history is unusually layered. Scheduled-Caste and Scheduled-Tribe safeguards intersected with backward-class commissions, the Karpoori Thakur formula, Mandal politics, a statutory division between Extremely Backward Classes and Backward Classes, women’s and other horizontal reservations, local-government quotas, welfare…

mai.title: आरक्षण, सकारात्मक कार्रवाई आ नव मध्यवर्ग
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आरक्षण, सकारात्मक कार्रवाई आ नव मध्यवर्ग” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: The Constitution transformed exclusion into a question of public representation
Scheduled-Caste and Scheduled-Tribe reservation opened early channels into the postcolonial state
Bihar’s backward-class question preceded the national Mandal moment
The Karpoori formula institutionalised unequal backwardness within the backward classes

en.title: Rural Elites, Political Economy and Changing Landed Power
en.summary: Rural power in Mithila, Vajji and Anga has never been reducible to acreage alone. Before independence, large estates, subordinate tenures, rent collection, credit, caste standing and access to officials could be concentrated in the same hands. After independence the legal architecture changed radically: intermediary interests were abolished, Bhoodan sought voluntary redistribution, ceiling legislation authorised acquisition of surplus land, electoral democracy widened political competition, and later panchayat…

mai.title: ग्रामीण अभिजन, राजनीतिक अर्थव्यवस्था आ बदलैत भूमिधारी शक्ति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “ग्रामीण अभिजन, राजनीतिक अर्थव्यवस्था आ बदलैत भूमिधारी शक्ति” विषयक जाति-वर्ग, दलित-आदिवासी-मुस्लिम इतिहास, परिवार, महिला श्रम, विवाह, शिक्षा आ ग्रामीण शक्तिक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Rural elite power must be analysed as a bundle of resources, not as landownership alone
The colonial agrarian order concentrated revenue authority and social power in layered intermediaries
Darbhanga Raj exemplifies the scale of estate power without representing all of Mithila
The Bihar Land Reforms Act of 1950 attacked intermediary rights rather than all private landed inequality
